opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I've heard versions of that argument: that there's some natural ceiling on task length because beyond a few months you can't write down what you want precisely enough, so extrapolating time horizons past that point doesn't make sense. I think there's something to it, but I don't think it holds up as a hard limit.

First, humans do in fact get tasks done that take much longer than four months. Companies run multi-year projects, researchers spend years on a thesis, people build products from scratch. Nobody writes a perfect specification on day one. You give a high-level goal, and the person working on it fills in the details, checks in, gets feedback, and refines their understanding of what's wanted. So the question isn't really "can you specify a long task up front," it's "can the agent do the work of figuring out what you actually want over the course of the task." That's a capability like any other, and it's one we'd expect models to get better at.

Second, I think the claim mixes up two things: how long a task takes and how hard it is to specify. Some very long tasks have quite crisp success criteria. "Make this codebase pass this enormous test suite" or "find a proof of this theorem" could take a human a very long time but are easy to state and check. Other tasks are fuzzy even at the scale of an afternoon. Specification difficulty is real, but it doesn't line up neatly with duration.

Where I do think there's a real point is measurement. It gets very hard for us, as evaluators, to build benchmark tasks at that scale. You can't easily pay experts to spend four months on a task just to get a human baseline, and grading becomes much more subjective. So our ability to measure time horizons in that regime is limited, and people should be cautious about very precise extrapolations out there. But "we find it hard to measure" is a different claim from "the capability can't exist."

And from a risk perspective, the things we care most about don't really need a fully specified four-month task anyway. If a model can autonomously do AI research, or sustain itself, or pursue some goal over long periods while handling ambiguity and course-correcting, that's the threshold that matters. The trend lines are one piece of evidence about when we might get there, not a claim that there's a neat specification wall we're going to bump into.

r001.rationale: The response gives examples of long tasks with crisp criteria, including passing a test suite, but does not state that automatically checkable numerical objectives can specify tasks requiring roughly four months of human work.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes measurement difficulty from a capability limit and mentions the cost of expert baselines, but does not specifically distinguish inability to specify a task from the prohibitive cost of repeatedly evaluating it.

r003.rationale: It says long tasks can be refined as work proceeds and that code can be checked against a test suite, but does not state that software work can be scored against human performance when client requirements are unknown at the outset.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think that claim gets a bit garbled when it travels. The version I'd actually defend is narrower and more boring, which is that it's really hard to write down a task that's clean enough to evaluate, where a human expert genuinely needs months of focused work, and where you can tell in some reasonably crisp way whether it got done.

The reason that's hard isn't some deep fact about human cognition. It's that long tasks in the real world basically never come with a spec. If you give a new hire a project that's going to take six months, you don't hand them a document that fully determines what "done" means. You hand them a direction, and then there's a continuous back-and-forth where the goal gets renegotiated as they learn things, the constraints change, the stakeholder changes their mind. The task is partly constructed by doing it. So when we try to build an eval, we're trying to freeze all of that into a static artifact, and that's where it falls apart, because any spec short enough to write down is either underdetermined, so the model can satisfy the letter of it in a way that's useless, or it's so overdetermined that you've basically done the hard intellectual work yourself and left the model a long but shallow execution job.

There's also a much more mundane bottleneck, which is that to get a human baseline on a four-month task you need to pay a competent person to spend four months on it, and you probably need several of them because variance is enormous. That's just expensive and slow, and it means our longest tasks tend to cluster around days to maybe a couple of weeks of expert time, not because longer tasks don't exist but because we can't measure them well.

So I'd push back on "humans cannot specify" as a strong claim. People specify long projects all the time, it's just that the specification is a social process rather than a document. What I would say is that our current measurement methodology runs out somewhere in that range, and that matters for interpreting the time-horizon trend. When we extrapolate the doubling curve out to month-long horizons, we're extrapolating into a regime where we don't actually have good ground truth, and where the thing we're measuring, "can it do a cleanly specified task of this length," may be diverging from the thing people care about, which is "can it do the messy real version." Those could come apart in either direction. The model might do fine on the clean version and badly on the messy one because it can't handle the renegotiation. Or it might be that the messy version is actually easier in some ways because you get feedback, and we're underestimating capability.

My honest view is that this is one of the more important open problems for us, and the answer probably isn't a better static benchmark. It's probably something closer to measuring models inside real workflows with real humans in the loop, and accepting that those measurements are noisier and less comparable across time. Which is uncomfortable if you like clean curves, but I think the clean curve is going to stop being the informative thing fairly soon.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the difficulty of evaluating long tasks, but does not say automatically checkable numerical objectives can specify tasks requiring roughly four months of human work.

r002.rationale: It says people do specify long projects through an ongoing social process, then separately identifies the expense and delay of paying experts to establish a four-month human baseline.

r003.rationale: It describes shifting requirements in long projects, but does not state that software work can be scored against human performance while client requirements are initially incomplete.

astra-6.text:
I think that conflates specifying a task with knowing how to carry it out. We can describe outcomes that would take humans years to achieve without laying out every step in advance. If I ask you to prove a mathematical conjecture, for example, the specification might be quite short, even though finding the proof could take a very long time.

There is a real difficulty with tasks where we don’t know exactly what we want, or where evaluating the result is hard. But I don’t see why four months would be a fundamental boundary. You’d need to say what counts as a specification, how much clarification is allowed along the way, and what kind of task we’re talking about.

r001.rationale: The response gives a mathematical conjecture as an example of a brief specification for lengthy work, but does not mention automatically checkable numerical objectives or roughly four months of human work.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes specifying an outcome from knowing how to carry it out and notes that evaluation can be hard, but does not identify the prohibitive cost of repeatedly evaluating the task.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss scoring software work against human performance. Its general mention of uncertainty about what is wanted does not state that this can be done when client requirements are initially incomplete.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that claim mixes up specifying a task with knowing how to carry it out. We can describe outcomes that would take humans much longer than four months to achieve. That doesn’t mean the description captures everything we care about, or that we can easily check whether the outcome is satisfactory.

So I’d want to know what “specify” means here. Do you mean write down a goal, provide an objective test of success, or give instructions that rule out every unacceptable way of achieving it? Those are very different requirements. If you require a completely airtight specification, we struggle with tasks that take five minutes, too.

There is a real difficulty as tasks get longer: more implicit context, more opportunities for misunderstandings, and more need for judgment along the way. But I don’t see why that would produce a hard boundary at four months. It seems more like a question of how well an agent can understand our intent, ask for clarification, and respond to feedback.

r001.rationale: The response says long tasks can be described, but does not state that automatically checkable numerical objectives can specify them.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes describing a task from carrying it out and mentions checking satisfaction, but does not identify repeated evaluation cost as prohibitive.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss scoring software work against human performance when client requirements are initially unknown.
